articles.title_orig: Xi Jinping got the red carpet treatment from Trump - but not everything he wanted
articles.title_zh: Xi Jinping got the red carpet treatment from Trump - but not everything he wanted
articles.content_orig:
Watch: The worldâs two most powerful men just met. How did it go?
President Xi Jinping's summits with Donald Trump have one clear aim.
China believes the United States is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan.
On this visit, however, despite Trump rolling out the red carpet for him, the Chinese leader didn't get everything he wanted.
The trade truce that saw both countries pause a tit-for-tat tariff war and prevent a further escalation, was extended by only a few months - from November to January.
Beijing had hoped for at least a year as Xi looks to ride out the remainder of Trump's presidency.
This means key disputes on tariffs, China's dominance on rare earth supplies and access to advanced US chips are being kicked forward into yet another round of negotiations.
This suggests the US wants China to do more to fulfil its side of the bargain before offering longer-term concessions.
Trump and Xi attend a dinner at the White House
The uncomfortable truth for Xi is that his domestic economy is in trouble. While the country sells a record number of goods around the world, consumers at home are holding back. Youth unemployment remains stubbornly high and property prices have slumped in a country where 80% of people own their own homes.
Trade is helping to prop up growth, making access to overseas markets more important than ever. Xi needs to protect those exports from the kind of debilitating tariffs the US imposed last year.
On Taiwan, Xi once again made clear that US arms sales to Taiwan are a red line for China.
The US is bound by law to provide the self-governing island with the means to defend itself.
In May, Xi warned Trump that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict".
Trump then delayed the approval of a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, describing it as a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing.
Xi may have seized on that opening during the talks and likely argued that restraining support for Taiwan reduces the risk of conflict.
On Thursday he reiterated his hope that the US would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence.
However,  Trump - who is coming under some bipartisan pressure to continue US support to Taiwan - is yet to make any public response to the Chinese leader's comments.
Trade is helping to prop up growth
The two leaders did at least discuss artificial intelligence (AI) although it's unclear whether they agreed to any safeguards.
All eyes were on whether they would make any concrete decisions on AI - such as an agreement to hold a summit - in the wake of an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for the slowing down of AI development to make it safer. That followed a warning by a top safety researcher from the company that there was a "greater than 10% chance" that AI could cause the extinction of humans.
But besides Xi talking about the importance of ensuring AI "is always under human control" we didn't get much else. Trump has most recently dismissed fears of human extinction from the technology as a "hoax".
And, of course, let's not forget the pandas . The gift of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to Atlanta was first heralded in April, but Xi has now announced they will arrive in just a few days as China's panda diplomacy resumes.
There may be more announcements to come as the two prepare to have tea and visit the national archives on Friday.
Pandas have played an important role in Chinese diplomatic measures
But for now, one of the summit's biggest victories for Beijing may have been the optics.
The lavish welcome, a personal greeting at the airport and a state banquet featuring sesame crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy have been welcomed by those watching from China. It will have helped cement Xi's image at home as Trump's equal.
Memes contrasting the two leaders have spread widely on Chinese social media. One popular image shows Trump grimacing as bomber jets fly overhead, while Xi remained impassive.
Xi has found a way to manage one of the world's most unpredictable leaders. But while Trump talks of a "truly great friendship", China's leader is focussed on something bigger: securing China's place alongside the United States as a superpower.
The pandas, the pageantry and the warm words may help smooth this relationship. But beneath the spectacle, the competition between the world's two most powerful countries remains as fierce as ever.

articles.title_orig: Atlanta is getting pandas: China's Xi revives a longtime diplomatic strategy at summit with U.S.
articles.title_zh: Atlanta is getting pandas: China's Xi revives a longtime diplomatic strategy at summit with U.S.
articles.content_orig:
Chinese leader Xi Jinping promised two giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta, reviving Beijing's decades-old charm offensive on the opening day of his first state visit to the U.S. in more than a decade.
Two giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, from a research base in Chengdu will arrive at the Georgia zoo "in the coming days," Xi said. They would be Zoo Atlanta's first pandas since its previous four returned to China in November 2024, when it became the last U.S. zoo to lose its bears.
The Chinese president made the announcement at the start of his state visit in Washington, where he and President Donald Trump are meeting through Friday on an agenda spanning artificial intelligence, tariffs, critical minerals, Taiwan and the Iran war.
"The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and Americans," he said at a White House ceremony.
China has used pandas as a diplomatic barometer since Mao Zedong sent a pair to Washington's National Zoo following Richard Nixon's 1972 visit, a gift so anticipated that more than a million people came to see the animals in their first year.
Beijing shifted from gifting pandas outright to leasing them in 1984, and the loans have since tracked the temperature of the relationship — thinning as trade and Taiwan tensions rose, then resuming as San Diego and the Washington DC National Zoo took in new pairs in 2024.
Pandas on loan to the U.S. have bred 17 cubs, including six in San Diego, four in Washington and seven in Atlanta, according to Chinese state media .
"Panda diplomacy conveys a message of friendship and goodwill from China," said Wu Xinbo, director of the Center for American Studies at Fudan University. "Americans may not like China, but they will certainly like pandas."
The gesture would improve the atmosphere between the world's two largest economies and generate positive momentum in bilateral relations, he said.
Experts have kept expectations muted for a summit likely to yield few major deliverables , even as the leaders' first meeting carries real geopolitical risk.
"For Beijing, the message is friendship without requiring major policy concessions. For Washington, it's a reminder that even amid intense competition, there is room for visible, people-to-people engagement," said Han Shen Lin, associate professor at NYU Shanghai.
Xi also said China would invite 100,000 young Americans to study there over the next five years.
Trump greeted Xi planeside at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, a welcome rarely extended to visiting heads of state. It is Xi's first state visit to the U.S. since Barack Obama's presidency more than a decade ago. He arrived in the U.S. on Wednesday and is scheduled to leave Friday.

articles.title_orig: Trump rolls out red carpets for Xi Jinping, though he has portrayed China as a global menace
articles.title_zh: Trump rolls out red carpets for Xi Jinping, though he has portrayed China as a global menace
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — He has accused China of hacking America’s elections and plundering its wealth, yet President Donald Trump has showered the visiting Chinese leader, Xi Jinping , with tributes and affection during their summit meeting this week at the White House.
Trump met his Chinese counterpart on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, outside Washington on Wednesday rather than wait back at the White House for an official greeting. It’s the first time he has ever shown a visiting world leader that courtesy.
Trump rolled out a red carpet not once but twice for Xi. The leaders walked side by side down a 100-foot-long red carpet after Xi’s Air China plane landed at Andrews. Another red carpet was laid out Thursday morning when Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, arrived at the White House for the summit’s first full day.
In the evening, Trump feted Xi at a state dinner whose menu included sesame-crusted sea bass and braised bok choy, followed by a dessert of vanilla crémeux and honey ice cream.
“As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better since the first trade ships from New York left the harbor to arrive on the banks of the Pearl River,” Trump said at the dinner.
He gave his guest a statue of a bald eagle as a gift.
All the pomp and ceremony might appear unusual given Trump’s past complaints that China has meddled in elections and exploited the U.S. through trade. Just two months ago, Trump gave a rare primetime speech asserting that China interfered in the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden.
But Trump, who has long believed that personal relationships are key to managing geopolitical tensions, has set out to charm the Chinese leader.
“From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship — a truly great friendship, actually — built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people,” Trump said Thursday morning in joint public statements he and Xi made before they held a private meeting in the Oval Office.
Xi struck a cordial tone in his remarks, saying he and Trump have developed a “personal rapport and stayed in touch.”
He also made an announcement certain to delight American children and anyone who has ever logged on to a panda-cam feed for a respite from life’s pressures: China will soon send two giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shang, to the Atlanta zoo, Xi said.
In an unusual rebuke from a member of Trump’s own party, Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., chairman of the Armed Services Committee, said Wednesday in a speech on the Senate floor that, “quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America, based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party.”
President Trump in landmark meeting with China’s leader
China may also have aided Iran in the war with the U.S. An F-15 fighter jet that was shot down over Iran in April was most likely hit by a Chinese-made shoulder-launched missile, three people familiar with the matter told NBC News . And in the early days of the seven-month-old conflict, China may have given Iran radar capabilities to help spot stealth aircraft, according to one of the people and a U.S. official with knowledge of the matter.
Honoring the leader of the world’s largest communist country may also undercut an argument Trump has made to discredit Democrats in the midterm elections. He has warned repeatedly that Democratic candidates would steer the U.S. in a communist direction if they are elected.
Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, told NBC News on Thursday, “I personally look at the red-carpet treatment and thought it was a little bit over the top.”
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said in an interview that while he didn’t mind seeing Xi thrown a dinner, “I don’t think the president ought to believe his bull----.”
After the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, the Iranian regime exerted a chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz , a crucial shipping lane for oil supplies.
Xi “could open up that strait with a phone call, and in a myriad of ways, he is helping Iran with military equipment, intelligence,” Kennedy said. “The guy learned to lie before he learned to talk.”
China, which has criticized the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and called for diplomatic negotiations, denies supplying Iran with weapons or military equipment.
No substantive breakthroughs are expected at the summit, foreign policy experts said. The two presidents were set to discuss trade, the Iran war and artificial intelligence , among other issues that have divided the U.S. and China. Trump entered the summit in a weakened posture, experts said, vexed by the prolonged Iran war and looming midterm congressional elections in which his party could lose its slim majority. He lacks the leverage needed to wring concessions from China, experts said.
Mark Montgomery, a retired Navy admiral, said at a pre-summit event hosted by the FDD think tank: “We have a president entering this playing a weak hand. I’m not 100% sure President Trump knows he’s playing a weak hand. I am 100% sure that leader Xi knows Trump is playing a weak hand.”
One area of cooperation might be the creation of a hotline that the U.S. and China could use to cope with an emergency arising from rapidly evolving AI technology , Secretary of State Marco Rubio suggested in an interview on “Fox & Friends” this week.
“It’s not a bad idea; it’s one that we’ll explore with the Chinese, among others,” Rubio said.
Along with closed-door meetings, Trump made a point to show off his prized White House projects. He took Xi outside to see the helipad he built on the South Lawn. Both men pointed down at the granite base.
When the leaders passed the press corps at one point, Trump said, “We had a great meeting.” He said Xi was “an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite.”
Walking with Xi along the West Wing Colonnade, Trump pointed to his “Presidential Walk of Fame” — pictures and biographical accounts of former presidents. He paused at the portrait of Biden, showing how he has mocked Biden by referring to him as “Autopen,” the device that presidents have used when they don’t have time to sign their own names to documents. A video snippet released by the White House shows the two presidents chuckling at the picture of Biden , with Trump giving Xi a friendly pat on the arm.
Confronting Xi in the moment may prove difficult for Trump. Xi is president for life; Trump is a president at risk of losing his governing majority in Congress. His approval rating has hit a second-term low .
One source of Xi’s leverage is his hold over rare earth materials , which are used in high-tech manufacturing. Last year, Trump slapped China with steep tariffs, igniting a trade war. Trump has long complained that China’s trade policies have bled the U.S. of wealth.
A statement from the White House in April 2025, tied to Trump’s “ Liberation Day ” tariffs, said Chinese practices “have given China global dominance in key manufacturing industries, decimating U.S. industry.”
But China’s command of rare earth supplies has proved an effective countermeasure, a resource the Trump administration can’t afford to lose. The two sides agreed to a trade truce last year, and on Wednesday they agreed to extend it two months, from Nov. 10 to Jan. 10.
Viewers who wanted to watch the summit live faced unusual difficulties following a media ban that Trump imposed last week. He barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from entering the White House grounds, prompting them to sue to regain access.

Olena Kalynychenko was looking forward to sharing the chrysanthemum tea she had bought in China with her partner.
“She said, ‘When I come back home, we will drink the tea made from Chinese flowers,’” said Oles Visich, Kalynychenko’s partner. He has now been waiting for news about her for a month, after she and thousands of others disappeared in catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border.
Her last known location was exiting China at a border post at 10:22 a.m. local time, 15 minutes before the flood.
Kalynychenko, 36, was part of a group of 56 people, mostly Ukrainians, who had traveled to Mount Kailash in Tibet for a spiritual retreat.
Their families' situation is a sign of how complex and time-consuming the process is of rescuing, recovering and identifying victims lost to the disaster. Given the number of missing, the process will likely take months.
They disappeared while heading from China to Nepal on their way home. Some relatives say they have received no information from authorities. The Chinese government has told at least two families that their relatives left Chinese territory before the flood struck, but they haven't been able to confirm whether they entered Nepal as Nepal's immigration complex and its records were destroyed in the floods.
The floods killed more than 1,400 people and left more than 6,000 missing, most of them on the Nepali side of the border. Nepal has said that 636 foreign nationals remain missing, including 54 Ukrainians. China has reported 261 foreign nationals among the missing on its side, including one Ukrainian.
Families in Ukraine say most of them have not received any answers since realizing their relatives were among the missing.
“We only have the statistics that are being posted online — how many people have been found, how many are alive, how many are dead, and how many are still missing,” said Stanislav Solohub, whose brother and sister-in-law went missing on Aug. 25.
Nepal says it has recovered 1,451 bodies, but only 112 have been handed over to families so far.
The government said it has collected DNA samples from 2,035 relatives so far, but it has not disclosed how many victims have been identified.
The group, led by Irina Blonskaya, a spiritual teacher who often organized retreats, was returning from its journey home in China when the flood struck Aug. 26. Their plan was to travel by bus from the Tibet region to Kathmandu , where its members would board flights to their respective countries. The group’s last message was sent at 8:27 a.m. Nepal time, about 10 minutes before the mountain slope collapsed.
Many had not checked in with their loved ones that morning, owing to the time difference.
Authorities have said the were triggered when a section of ice and rock broke away from a Himalayan mountain slope, creating a fast-moving torrent of water, ice, mud and debris. It destroyed communities and Gyirong Port, a border crossing used by some pilgrims traveling to or returning from Mount Kailash.
Vladsylava Horlova’s mother, Elena, was traveling in the group as well. She initially found her mother’s name of the list of the missing from the Nepali government, but hasn't received any further information from the Nepali side. Later, the Chinese embassy confirmed her mother had left the country, and was not counted in China's list of missing people.
Horlova, a college student who is a refugee in Norway , worries her mother wasn't in either country when the flood struck. There’s a stretch of road between the Nepali immigration building and the Chinese one along the border, videos from travelers show.
“You think about what if someone appeared to be in a no man’s land or that they left China, but not physically, who’s looking for them?” she asked.
Horlova has attempted to contact organizations ranging from the Ukrainian embassy in China, to Norwegian police, and even the Red Cross . She, like the others, have submitted their DNA samples to police to help the search.
On the other side of the border, China has said that when the remains of foreigners are identified, it will notify their respective embassies, but the authorities have not given any details about how many identities have been confirmed so far.
Though it has been a month since the original disaster, some families are still holding on to hope.
Just days before Kalynychenko left for her travels, she organized a retreat for women in Ukraine whose partners were fighting on the front lines of the war, some of whom had not heard from their partners for two years.
Visich, her partner, sees the irony of his situation, but like others in the group, has chosen to stay positive. Visich, also a psychologist, wrote a support guide for others like himself, offering tips on mental health.
“Because for my Olenka, for example, the most important thing in our connection, that each other … needs to be happy,” Visich said.

articles.title_orig: Cambridge Abandons Plans to Fully Investigate Its Hiring of Jason Arday
articles.title_zh: Cambridge Abandons Plans to Fully Investigate Its Hiring of Jason Arday
articles.content_orig:
Published : Sep 24, 2026 20:17 IST  - 11  MINS  READ
A photo of late Cambridge professor Jason Arday, along with floral tributes, attached to the fencing by supporters around the Senate House at the University of Cambridge, in the town of Cambridge, eastern England, on August 18, 2026.
                                          | Photo Credit: Chris Radburn/AFP
Jason Arday was appointed professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge in February 2023, becoming, at 37, the youngest Black person ever appointed to a professorship at the university. The appointment was widely celebrated across British academia as evidence of institutional progress, in a sector where Black professors remain starkly underrepresented. In 2024-25, Black academics accounted for just 1 per cent of professors in UK higher education.
In July 2026, allegations of plagiarism, questions about his research and disputes over claims in his biography triggered a wave of media investigations into his work and public account of his life. Cambridge subsequently announced an investigation into his academic qualifications and honorary appointments, alongside existing complaints concerning academic misconduct. Arday resigned on August 5, days after the scrutiny intensified, saying his resignation should not be “mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me”.
Nine days later, he was found unresponsive at his home in Battersea and pronounced dead, aged 41. An inquest subsequently opened after the coroner said there was reason to suspect an unnatural death. The inquest has been adjourned.
His case became a cultural battlefield over race, merit, diversity, representation and affirmative action. His exceptional visibility as Cambridge’s youngest Black professor was celebrated in British academia as evidence of institutional progress. At the same time, we need to think about how paradoxically intriguing his whole controversy was: the same visibility that was being celebrated made him disproportionately vulnerable to scrutiny and ideological attack.
Also Read | India’s equity rules are a court-mandated mirage
There lies a substantial danger when institutions treat the presence of a marginalised individual as evidence that inequality has been overcome; representation might become a spectacle rather than transformation. Arday’s case asks for a rethink in the narrative of representation as inclusivity. There is a need to distinguish between representation as structural justice, when communities historically discriminated against demand the spaces they were never allowed to participate in, and representation as institutional tokenism, where a marginalised person is allowed to participate in an institution for the sake of inclusivity.
The excessive publicity surrounding his appointment itself illustrates a paradox: he was simultaneously recognised and othered. He was simply not allowed to be a scholar; he became a symbol of diversity, resilience, and institutional liberalism.
Many fail to see the underlying consequences such identity politics might produce and, in Arday’s case, the consequences explicitly came to the surface. It could be understood as “ghettoisation through representation”, where once an individual from a marginalised community becomes a symbol, their individuality is rendered secondary to the political function they perform for the institution. What happens when such individuals get to exercise their own agency within this contemporary diversity politics? Do they remain only as representatives of diversity? Identity politics cannot be dismissed altogether on account of such questions.
Asserting one’s identity through identity politics does not explicitly mean ghettoisation; in fact, identities which are “invisible” or have been historically invisibilised could utilise the very identity politics as a form of assertion. But the larger critique should ask whether mere institutional representation can be considered emancipation in itself. Do marginalised individuals still get to practise their agency via inclusive or diverse safeguards? Perhaps it’s intriguing to think that ghettoisation might not always occur through exclusion; sometimes, paradoxically, it occurs through inclusion itself.
Supporters take part in a vigil for late Cambridge professor Jason Arday in Trafalgar Square in central London on August 17, 2026.
                                                            | Photo Credit: 
                                Carlos Jasso/AFP
The Dalit scholar becomes the “Dalit academic”; the Black professor becomes the “Black success story”; the disabled student becomes an inspirational narrative. Their intellectual identity is constantly subordinated to their social identity. They are made hypervisible as members of a community but not recognised as autonomous intellectuals.
This produces a peculiar form of institutional violence. The privileged individual is allowed the luxury of being mediocre, complex, contradictory, or simply ordinary, but the marginalised individual must constantly justify their presence. Their failure is never merely individual; it is made representative of the supposed inadequacy of their entire community. Nobody would argue that the existence of a corrupt uppered-caste* professor proves that uppered castes are incapable of academic excellence, yet the failure of one reserved-category candidate is routinely mobilised as evidence against reservation itself. Such individuals, therefore, are denied the right to individual failure; they are simply not allowed the luxury of failure. Their failure is projected as an incapacity produced by the very communities they belong to. Affirmative action and representative politics carry this political violence within them, but the problem is not representation itself; it is the politics surrounding it, be it left wing or right wing.
The political Right attacks affirmative action through the language of meritocracy . It portrays reservation as an undeserved privilege and an assault on excellence. But this conception of merit deliberately forgets history: merit is never produced in a social vacuum. Who attends better schools? Who has educated parents? Who is surrounded by professional networks and intergenerational familiarity with universities? Such questions reveal who decides merit. Caste and racial privileges become invisible in the heap of merit.
This is where an Ambedkarite intervention becomes particularly necessary. B.R. Ambedkar , the anti-caste reformer and principal architect of India’s Constitution, demanded separate electorates for the Depressed Classes, the term then used for communities now broadly identified as Dalits. The British government’s Communal Award of 1932 granted separate electorates, but the Poona Pact of September 1932 replaced them with reserved seats within joint electorates.
It is crucial to understand that Ambedkar considered reservation a teleological tool, meaning a means directed towards a larger end, that would change the lives of Dalits in India, but he never considered it an emancipatory tool in itself.
Perhaps this is precisely why the same critique needs extending to the liberal Left. The political Left should not be treated as automatically emancipatory. Liberal and Left institutions often celebrate representation while refusing to transform their own internal structures. They celebrate the marginalised as evidence, or a token, of their own progress but grow uncomfortable when the same individual challenges their institutional power and hegemony.
Institutional discrimination does not simply vanish because a progressive Left politician comes to power. In India, we cannot forget the case of Chuni Kotal, an Adivasi woman of the Lodha community of West Bengal. A photo shared by President Donald Trump from his meeting with Chinese Leader Xi Jinping has caused questions and speculation throughout the internet.
On Thursday, Trump shared the photo on his Truth Social platform . In it, the president stands next to Xi, with Trump’s arm raised in a salute. The words “Only Trump” are in the picture as the two leaders stand in the foreground at the front of the red carpet with Xi’s plane in the background. Overhead, a military plane flies past the scene.
A lone woman is also caught in the picture. Some on the internet have speculated that is was Trump’s personal aide Natalie Harp . But the woman is Chief of Protocol Monica Crowley , a former Fox News anchor who joined the Trump administration.
Others have questioned if the photo was made by AI. Trump was mocked for flinching during the flyover, and was caught by cameras clenching his teeth and ducking his head . Others pointed out other issues with the picture, such as Trump missing a glove on one hand, but it appearing in other pictures from the event. In addition, the shoes Crowley was seen wearing in the original Reuters photograph – similar to Mary Janes with a horizontal strap across the top – appear to have been changed to classic nude-colored pumps in the picture posted on Truth Social.
Notably absent from the picture shared on Truth Social was first lady Melania Trump, who was also present at the event.
A number of social media users questioned whether the photo had been manipulated, whether through AI or other means.
“Why take the glove off his left hand??” wrote one X user. In pictures taken by photojournalists, the president can be seen wearing two black gloves.
“There’s a lot of slop,” another user chimed in.
“He AI edited out his wife but left Natalie?” questioned a third user, though the woman in the photo is actually Crowley.
Crowley has served as U.S. chief of protocol since 2025, advising the president on diplomatic protocol.
She has accompanied Trump during other meetings with other world leaders, including King Charles III and Queen Camilla . She also traveled with Trump to Beijing for his state visit in May.
On Thursday, Trump and Xi struck a positive tone about their relationship and outlined areas for cooperation as the state visit got underway.
“From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship, actually, built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people,” Trump said. He added that the two leaders would discuss artificial intelligence and other pressing issues.
Xi said he and Trump had established a “personal rapport” and called for closer diplomatic ties in order to bring about a peaceful coexistence.
“It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses,” the Chinese leader said.
An earlier version of this story and headline incorrectly identified the person in the photo as Donald Trump's personal aide Natalie Harp. The person in the frame is Chief of Protocol Monica Crowley.

CNN is one of the five major networks that provide pool video coverage of White House events to other broadcasters, in a rotation determined by the White House press office.

Footage captures the tense moment of impact between a Chinese Coast Guard ship and a Philippine fisheries vessel in the South China Sea. (Video one credit: Chinese Coast Guard)
Tensions in the South China Sea escalated again Friday after a Chinese Coast Guard vessel collided with a Philippine government ship, an encounter captured on video that prompted competing accounts from Manila and Beijing.
The Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources vessel BRP Datu Magat Salamat was distributing fuel to Filipino fishermen when the collision occurred at 11:13 a.m., roughly 54 nautical miles off the coast of Palawan province — an area Manila says is well within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone.
Footage released by the Philippine Coast Guard showed crew members shouting, "Brace for impact!" moments before the collision. Photographs taken afterward showed bent and detached railings, damaged metal supports and debris scattered across the Philippine ship's deck. No injuries were reported.

A Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources vessel, labeled DA-BFAR MMOV 3015, navigates in proximity to another ship during a maritime encounter. (Chinese Coast Guard )
Philippine officials accused Beijing of deliberately ramming a civilian government vessel on what they described as a humanitarian and livelihood mission.
Jay Tarriela, the Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson for West Philippine Sea concerns, said the Chinese vessel first cut across the Philippine ship's stern at a distance of about 33 feet before repeating the maneuver minutes later and colliding with it.
Two Philippine Coast Guard ships were reportedly surrounded by Chinese vessels in a tense standoff in the South China Sea on March 24, 2025. (Philippine Coast Guard (PCG)/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Beijing disputed Manila's account. Chinese Coast Guard spokesperson Jiang Lue said the Philippine vessel "intentionally adjusted its course and suddenly accelerated to cut across the bow" of the Chinese ship after disregarding repeated warnings. China said its vessel had been conducting lawful operations near Sabina Shoal and blamed the Philippine side for the collision.
Philippine resupply vessel Unaizah May 4, center, is hit by two Chinese coast guard water cannons as they tried to enter the Second Thomas Shoal in the disputed South China Sea on March 5, 2024. (AP Photo/Aaron Favila, File)
The incident also drew Washington into the dispute. U.S. Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said the United States "strongly condemn[s] the China Coast Guard's deliberate ramming."
The Chinese Embassy in Manila responded by accusing the United States of backing Philippine "infringement and provocations" in the disputed waters.

Friday's collision was the latest in a series of maritime confrontations between China and the Philippines. In July, Manila accused Chinese forces of firing water cannons at government vessels near Scarborough Shoal and striking a Philippine Navy staff member in the head with a wooden baton during an encounter at Second Thomas Shoal.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said it is up to the U.S. to decide whether to end their seven-month war, amid continued missile strikes in the Middle East and a fresh push by China to help broker a peace resolution.
"It's America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not," Pezeshkian said, responding to a question about whether the war could end by year-end, in an interview aired Thursday on Fox News.
The remarks came as the Houthis fired dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi targets on Friday morning, according to Saudi authorities, who said they intercepted six ballistic missiles.
Emergency alerts were issued in Mecca, Jeddah and Yanbu. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan planned an urgent meeting of their chiefs of staff to discuss ways to support the kingdom under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
Pezeshkian has sought to distance Tehran from the escalation, telling Fox News "the Houthis are responsible for their own actions" and that Iran is "not at war with Saudi Arabia." The Houthis, he said, "have their own issues."
Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti struck a starkly different tone , telling troops to be ready "to lay down their lives" to fight the Houthis until the group is ousted from power.
The widening front has kept oil markets on edge. Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for November delivery declined 1% at $93.66 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November dropped 0.68% at $105.86 per barrel.
Vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz, normally the route for about a fifth of global oil supply, fell to 9, far below peacetime levels, according to Reuters , citing preliminary ship-tracking data showed on Friday.
Diplomatically, the war has become entangled with this week's U.S.-China summit in Washington. Chinese President Xi Jinping is on a three-day state visit to the U.S., meeting with President Donald Trump on issues spanning trade, artificial intelligence, Taiwan and Iran.
Zhai Jun, China's special envoy for the Middle East, said at an event in Singapore that "the Middle East situation was a big issue in the leaders' discussion that just took place, and the consensus they reached there will be critical to cooling the temperature in the conflict."
Trump has sought Beijing's help pressuring Tehran toward a settlement, after indirect U.S.-Iran talks resumed on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week. Iranian officials have signaled they could reopen the Strait within seven days, if Washington begins easing its naval blockade of Iranian ports.

articles.title_orig: Bob Pettit, basketball great who was named the NBA’s first MVP, dies at 93
articles.title_zh: Bob Pettit, basketball great who was named the NBA’s first MVP, dies at 93
articles.content_orig:
Bob Pettit, an imposing scorer and rebounder for the St. Louis Hawks and winner of the NBA's first Most Valuable Player award in 1956, has died. He was 93.
Pettit's alma mater, LSU, announced Thursday that he died a day earlier. The university did not provide a cause of death.
Pettit was an All-American at LSU before going on to the NBA, where he was an All-Star for each of his 11 seasons, all with the Hawks. He led them to the 1958 championship over the mighty Boston Celtics, the Hawks' lone title.
He was also the NBA MVP in 1959 and was the MVP of the All-Star Game four times, an achievement matched only by Los Angeles Lakers great Kobe Bryant.
Pettit was a force at a time when the NBA featured the likes of Wilt Chamberlain, Bill Russell, Oscar Robertson and Elgin Baylor. But it was also before a time when the NBA was widely seen on television, and Pettit — playing in a smaller market — was denied a larger audience.
At 6-foot-9 and 205 pounds and with a deeply receding hairline, Pettit was a physical presence at power forward, before such a position became part of basketball's vocabulary. He rarely missed a game. He also played center and was one of the first big men who did not play solely with his back to the basket.
Pettit was the Rookie of the Year in 1955, the last year the Hawks played in Milwaukee before moving to St. Louis.
He captured the MVP the next season, leading the league in scoring at 25.7 points a game. He also was the NBA's scoring leader in 1959 at 29.2 points.
He retired after the 1964-65 season with career averages of 26.4 points and 16.2 rebounds. At that time, he was the NBA's career leader in points (20,880) and second in rebounds (12,849).
He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 1970.
"Lean, graceful, and always well-conditioned, Bob Pettit's physical build made him one of the first big men to play facing the basket," reads Pettit's biographical profile at the Hall of Fame. "But Pettit's resolve set him apart from his peers; he simply would not be outworked."
Robert Lee Pettit Jr. was born on Dec. 12, 1932, in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. His father worked in law enforcement and served as East Baton Rouge Parish sheriff. Pettit was a late bloomer in basketball, not making the Baton Rouge High School varsity until his junior season.
As a senior, he led Baton Rouge to a state championship and wound up with more than a dozen college offers. He chose to stay home and starred at LSU as a sophomore, an era when players could not join the varsity until then.
He led the Southeastern Conference in scoring all three of his seasons, with averages of 25.5 points as a sophomore, 24.9 as a junior and 31.4 as a senior.
Pettit is one of only three LSU players — Pete Maravich and Shaquille O'Neal the others — to earn a place in the Hall of Fame. Bronze statues of Pettit and O'Neal stand outside LSU's home arena, the Pete Maravich Assembly Center. His No. 50 is retired by LSU, his No. 9 by the Atlanta Hawks.
Pettit's misfortune was that most of his career coincided with a run of Celtics championships that remains one of the most dominant runs in American pro sports history.
Pettit was two victories short of being a three-time NBA champion. Pettit's Hawks advanced to the finals four times, all against Boston, twice losing in seven games.
The first meeting, won by Boston in 1957, came down to double overtime of Game 7. The second ended with a championship for the Hawks, interrupting Boston's run of nine titles in 10 seasons. The Hawks also dropped NBA Finals matchups with the Celtics in 1960 (in seven games) and 1961 (in five).
Pettit retired to his native Baton Rouge after leaving basketball and worked in banking and financial consulting. He was a regular at LSU and New Orleans Pelicans games in recent years.

articles.content_orig:
Kayrasaurus changliensis is a newly discovered theropod dinosaur with giant claws and densely packed teeth
The dinosaur, found in China, lived approximately 125 million years ago and measured nearly 12 feet long
Researchers say it provides new insights into therizinosaurian evolution and ecological adaptations in the Jehol Biota
A new dinosaur believed to have roamed western China during the Early Cretaceous period has just been discovered.
Kayrasaurus changliensis is described as a "bizarre" theropod with giant claws that might look like a feathered bear if it were still alive today, Phys.org and Sci.News reported the week of Sept. 21.
The reports are "based on a nearly complete" skeleton that was "missing the hind limbs," according to a team of researchers who published their findings in the Journal of Systematic Palaeontology .
Several of the dinosaur's features have allowed experts to identify the K. changliensis as a new species, with "extremely small and densely packed teeth," which are "indicative of enhanced bite force and a more robust, less cursorial body plan."
Among the creature's distinctive features are "more strongly curved manual claws" on "three manual digits."
"The manual phalanges are relatively completely preserved," researchers said, adding that the medium-sized therizinosaurian also had "a dorsally extended 'lip.'"
K. changliensis was discovered in the Lower Cretaceous Yixian Formation of western Liaoning, China.
The name comes from " Kayra ," the god of creation in Turkic Shamanism, who is the father of Erlik, the god of death, "symbolizing its phylogenetic connection to Erlikosaurus ; saurus, Greek for lizard," per the Journal of Systematic Paleontology .
"The specific name changliensis is derived from Changli , a historical place name from the Three Kingdoms period, referring to the provenance of the fossil," the team of researchers continued.
Therizinosauria refers to an "anatomically bizarre and rare group of theropod dinosaurs," which had small heads and elongated necks.
Beipiaosaurus inexpectus , a roughly 7-foot long feathered herbivorous dinosaur, was previously believed to have been the largest of this particular therizinosaur group during this period until the K. changliensis came along at nearly double the size.
A skeletal diagram of Kayrasaurus changliensis. Credit: Journal of Systematic Palaeontology
Researchers believe the newly discovered dinosaur measured approximately 11.8 feet long and is estimated to have weighed between 258 and 604 pounds, Phys.org reported.
"As the largest therizinosaurian yet known from the Jehol Biota, K. changliensis bridges morphological gaps between previously described taxa," per the Journal of Systematic Palaeontology.
In drawings published in the journal, K. changliensis stands larger in comparison to other dinosaurs in its genus, including B. inexpectus , Lingyuanosaurus ( L. sihedangensis ), and Jianchangosaurus ( J. yixianensis ).

The researchers noted that their interpretations "remain provisional due to several limitations," and that research into the new discovery will continue.
K. changliensis lived around 125 million years ago.
"Kayrasaurus changliensis, together with the results of our phylogenetic analysis, provides new insights into the morphological evolution and ecological adaptations of therizinosaurians in the Jehol Biota," researchers said of the well-preserved Early Cretaceous fossil ecosystem in northeastern China.
"However, further analyses and the discovery of more complete, well-preserved specimens are essential to rigorously test and refine these hypotheses."
PEOPLE reached out to the researchers involved in the study for comment.

Nepal 's prime minister scolded fellow world leaders Thursday, saying the nation's recent deadly flood reminds a warming world that climate change keeps hurting people who didn't cause the crisis but now need help.
The August disaster “was not just a local tragedy. It was a warning to the world. And I ask you today: Have you really heard that warning?” Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah said at the U.N. General Assembly on Thursday night. “Nearly three years ago, standing in the shadow of our Mount Everest , the secretary-general of the United Nations warned about humanity about the madness and impending climate disaster.”
“That cry from the rooftop of the world was not heard enough,” Shah said. “We in Nepal heard it. Our communities heard it. Scientists around the world heard it. They repeated it with evidence. But we, the political leaders, have been negligent to translate those warnings in action at the speed and scale that the vulnerable people require.”
International scientists have connected melting permafrost from climate — caused by burning coal, oil and gas — to the instability of the glacier, which partly collapsed and triggered a massive flood that has killed at least 1,400 people with even more still missing.
Shah said that Nepal contributed less than one-tenth of 1% of the heat-trapping gases behind climate change. About 99% of Nepal's electricity comes from hydropower, and many workers were trapped in tunnels by the flooding.
“We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying a colossal price for it,” said Shah, 36, a former rapper and engineer who is the youngest head of government to address the General Assembly this year. “Our glaciers are retreating, our mountain slopes are becoming unstable, our rivers are becoming less predictable, and every major disaster threatens to erase years of development.”
He said climate change ‘does not recognize borders’
In a black Dhaka topi, a traditional brimless Nepali hat, Shah spoke while wearing his signature dark sunglasses, which he uses for medical reasons. He said “the tragic consequences of a warming climate” tells the world that “climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with stamps and passports.”
Subeksha Khadka, a humanitarian and former Miss Nepal International, in an online interview, praised Shah's speech and echoed the warning: "This time Nepal has been on the target, but it could be anyone. This is our story right now, and it can be anybody else’s tomorrow. So it’s time to act.”
Shah didn't ask for a specific amount in aid, but he called the international financial aid system inadequate and too bureaucratic. This included a loss and damage fund agreed upon a few years ago for poor nations hit by climate disasters not of their own making.
“Climate finance must not become another bureaucratic maze through which vulnerable countries spend years” maneuvering through when they need help. “When the house is burning, we do not ask a family to complete 50 forms. We act. This is what climate justice means.”
He exhorted the General Assembly to act on relief, rehabilitation, reconstruction — which are traditional international help concepts — but also “responsibility, reparation, resilience.” Reparation is a word and an issue that rankles industrial western nations like the United States , which is historically the world's biggest carbon emitter.
He says it's ‘not an isolated disaster’
Over the past 75 years, the United States has spewed about 1,500 times more carbon into the air than Nepal has, according to the Global Carbon Project, a group of scientists that track greenhouse gas emissions by countries. Historical emissions matter because carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere for more than a century trapping heat.
The U.S. this week announced $31 million in aid to Nepal for flood recovery, which bring America's total financial help up to $36 million. It's less than 1% of what they need.
“Preliminary assessments indicate that from recent disaster alone, Nepal has suffered loss of over $5 billion, nearly 15% of our GDP and a third of our annual budget," Shisir Khanal, Nepal's foreign minister, said Wednesday at the UN climate summit. "Thus for Nepal, this catastrophe is not merely a humanitarian emergency. It is a development emergency dismantling years of progress. It is a justice crisis exposing the inequities of global climate action and it is an existential crisis striking at the very survival of our communities and our future.”
“What happened in Nepal is not an isolated disaster but a preview of what awaits many vulnerable nations,” Khanal said.
Former United States Vice President Al Gore said in an interview that Nepal's disaster shows that the climate crisis “was getting worse much faster” than people can handle and foreshadows problems with melting glaciers that feed all of the great rivers of Asia, putting the water supply of 2 billion people at risk.
Delgado reported from New York. Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed to this report.

Watch: What's the latest on the White House media ban?
CNN and MS NOW reporters say they have been denied entry to cover a White House state dinner despite a judge ruling their access to the grounds must be restored.
A federal judge said in an overnight ruling that the White House ban on three outlets - CNN and MS NOW and Politico - was likely unconstitutional and that the administration must allow them access, for now. Trump barred them last week, accusing them of "fake news".
Journalists with the three outlets were allowed back in on Thursday morning.
Then in the evening, a CNN reporter and a producer and an MS NOW reporter said that they were denied entry to cover the guests arriving for a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
The outlets said they had properly submitted their reporters' names for credentials to cover the arrivals.
CNN said that about an hour before Xi was scheduled to arrive, the White House said it could cover the event only with a photojournalist and audio technician, but not a team that included a reporter and producer.
MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barron-Lopez said she was told by White House staff that she could not be let in, and to contact the White House communications director.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
A White House communications account posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event, and every press call".
The incident was the latest in a series of events on Thursday surrounding the ban on some media outlets at the White House.
Despite the overnight ruling, CNN, Politico and MS NOW all reported being denied entry to the White House on Thursday morning, prompting a request for an emergency court hearing.
In response, the director of White House Operations said in a court filing that the press passes and confiscated badges had been restored by 09:45 local time (13:45 GMT).
Shortly afterwards, all three outlets said they were allowed back in.
However, networks including Fox News, NBC, CBS and ABC, which pulled out in solidarity, have yet to confirm they will resume broadcast coverage from the White House.
The chaotic standoff limited some TV coverage as Trump welcomed Xi to the White House ahead of a state dinner.
CNN White House reporter Betsy Klein, seen here back at the White House on Thursday, was reportedly denied access earlier in the day
In his ruling, Judge Timothy Kelly said the ban on the outlets should be temporarily lifted because it "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".
He cast doubt on White House claims that the ban was justified in part on national security grounds, pointing out the president made no mention of this in his initial announcement.
"The record lacks factual support for defendants' contention that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security," Kelly wrote.
Judge Kelly ruled CNN, Politico and MS NOW were "likely to succeed" in showing the White House had not exercised "adequate due process" in the ban.
He ordered the immediate return of the outlets' press passes and a halt to enforcement of the ban for 14 days.
In a court filing on Tuesday, the US Department of Justice had accused the news outlets of threatening national security with their coverage.
Government lawyers cited stories about missile stockpiles, the construction of the White House ballroom and the recent Republican midterm convention.

Trump first announced last Friday he was barring the three outlets from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.
By Saturday morning, each outlet reported that they were denied entry to t he White House grounds and that their press badges were confiscated.
All three outlets accused the Trump administration of violating their constitutional rights.
In a joint statement on Monday, they said they were pursuing legal action to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports".
More than 50 media organisations across the ideological spectrum filed an amicus brief in support of the lawsuit, including Fox News, the New York Times, the Washington Post and the Wall Street Journal.
There have been previous instances of administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.
The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a specific press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.
But after objections from the other four networks in the press pool, Fox News was allowed in.

articles.title_orig: A month after Nepal-China floods, families await answers about more than 50 missing Ukrainians
articles.title_zh: A month after Nepal-China floods, families await answers about more than 50 missing Ukrainians
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK (AP) — Olena Kalynychenko was looking forward to sharing the chrysanthemum tea she had bought in China with her partner.
“She said, ‘When I come back home, we will drink the tea made from Chinese flowers,’” said Oles Visich, Kalynychenko’s partner. He has now been waiting for news about her for a month, after she and thousands of others disappeared in catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border.
Her last known location was exiting China at a border post at 10:22 a.m. local time, 15 minutes before the flood.
Kalynychenko, 36, was part of a group of 56 people, mostly Ukrainians, who had traveled to Mount Kailash in Tibet for a spiritual retreat.
Their families' situation is a sign of how complex and time-consuming the process is of rescuing, recovering and identifying victims lost to the disaster. Given the number of missing, the process will likely take months.
They disappeared while heading from China to Nepal on their way home. Some relatives say they have received no information from authorities. The Chinese government has told at least two families that their relatives left Chinese territory before the flood struck, but they haven't been able to confirm whether they entered Nepal as Nepal's immigration complex and its records were destroyed in the floods.
The floods killed more than 1,400 people and left more than 6,000 missing, most of them on the Nepali side of the border. Nepal has said that 636 foreign nationals remain missing, including 54 Ukrainians. China has reported 261 foreign nationals among the missing on its side, including one Ukrainian.
Families in Ukraine say most of them have not received any answers since realizing their relatives were among the missing.
“We only have the statistics that are being posted online — how many people have been found, how many are alive, how many are dead, and how many are still missing,” said Stanislav Solohub, whose brother and sister-in-law went missing on Aug. 25.
Nepal says it has recovered 1,451 bodies, but only 112 have been handed over to families so far.
The government said it has collected DNA samples from 2,035 relatives so far, but it has not disclosed how many victims have been identified.
The group, led by Irina Blonskaya, a spiritual teacher who often organized retreats, was returning from its journey home in China when the flood struck Aug. 26. Their plan was to travel by bus from the Tibet region to Kathmandu, where its members would board flights to their respective countries. The group’s last message was sent at 8:27 a.m. Nepal time, about 10 minutes before the mountain slope collapsed.
Many had not checked in with their loved ones that morning, owing to the time difference.
Authorities have said the were triggered when a section of ice and rock broke away from a Himalayan mountain slope, creating a fast-moving torrent of water, ice, mud and debris. It destroyed communities and Gyirong Port, a border crossing used by some pilgrims traveling to or returning from Mount Kailash.
Vladsylava Horlova’s mother, Elena, was traveling in the group as well. She initially found her mother’s name of the list of the missing from the Nepali government, but hasn't received any further information from the Nepali side. Later, the Chinese embassy confirmed her mother had left the country, and was not counted in China's list of missing people.
Horlova, a college student who is a refugee in Norway, worries her mother wasn't in either country when the flood struck. There’s a stretch of road between the Nepali immigration building and the Chinese one along the border, videos from travelers show.
“You think about what if someone appeared to be in a no man’s land or that they left China, but not physically, who’s looking for them?” she asked.
Horlova has attempted to contact organizations ranging from the Ukrainian embassy in China, to Norwegian police, and even the Red Cross. She, like the others, have submitted their DNA samples to police to help the search.
On the other side of the border, China has said that when the remains of foreigners are identified, it will notify their respective embassies, but the authorities have not given any details about how many identities have been confirmed so far.
Though it has been a month since the original disaster, some families are still holding on to hope.
Just days before Kalynychenko left for her travels, she organized a retreat for women in Ukraine whose partners were fighting on the front lines of the war, some of whom had not heard from their partners for two years.
Visich, her partner, sees the irony of his situation, but like others in the group, has chosen to stay positive. Visich, also a psychologist, wrote a support guide for others like himself, offering tips on mental health.
“Because for my Olenka, for example, the most important thing in our connection, that each other … needs to be happy,” Visich said.
AP writer Binaj Gurubacharya in Kathmandu, Nepal and senior video producer Volodymr Yurchuk in Kyiv, Ukraine contributed to this report.

Donald Trump just welcomed Xi Jinping back to the White House for a state dinner in honor of the Chinese leader that will not be televised because the White House continued to deny full access to the event to CNN journalists on Thursday, despite a court order.
Xi’s arrival for the dinner, with his wife Peng Liyuan, was streamed live on YouTube by the White House, but none of the major US networks provided live broadcast video of the event after the Trump administration refused to allow a CNN reporter and producer to cover the event.
“About an hour before Xi’s arrival was scheduled, the White House said CNN could cover the event but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, notably excluding the network’s editorial team consisting of a reporter and producer,” CNN reports .
CNN is one of the five major networks that provide pool video coverage of White House events to other broadcasters, in a rotation determined by the White House press office.
The other networks – ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News – have refused to resume video coverage of White House events until full access has been restored to CNN.
MS NOW, another outlet banned from the White House by Trump last week for what he calls overly negative coverage of his presidency, also reports it journalists were prevented from covering Xi’s arrival for the state dinner.
The live YouTube stream of Xi’s arrival attracted just 18,000 views on the White House YouTube channel.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping to the White House for a state dinner in honor of the Chinese leader that was not televised because the White House continued to deny full access to the event to CNN journalists on Thursday, despite a court order.
Writing on his social media platform, Trump complained that two of the three outlets he banned from the White House, CNN and MS Now, “refused to cover” his elaborate welcome of Xi to the White House. He did not mention that the two broadcasters were not in position to cover the event live because his own actions and those of his aides, who continued to block their reporters.
As Israel’s prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu attacked him at the UN, New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani , doubled down on his support for Palestinians by making public video of himself hosting Palestinian families from Gaza.
Darializa Avila Chevalier , the Democratic socialist congressional candidate from New York, was among dozens of activists arrested near the United Nations on Thursday at a protest against Netanyahu’s appearance organized by Jewish Voice for Peace.
The Trump administration used taxpayer funds to air a White House-produced, pro-Trump ad on Fox News this week.
The Trump administration used taxpayer funds to air a White House-produced, pro-Trump ad on Fox News this week, as Jim DeFede of CBS News Miami first reported .
The 30-second ad , which uses audio of Donald Trump telling supporters in Las Vegas last month: “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America,” includes a rapid-fire montage of images from his second term displayed beneath the on-screen text: “America will never be a communist country,” as a chorus sings the words “love me”, taken from a song of that name by JMSN.
The last 10 seconds of the ad includes text at the bottom the screen which says: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
It airs as Trump is hosting the leader of the world’s largest communist nation, China, for a lavish state visit.
In a statement provided to Politico , the White House described versions of the ad, which were also posted on official government accounts on TikTok and YouTube , as simply “public service announcements” that are “educational and unapologetically patriotic”.
In fact, the 30-second version of the ad broadcast on Fox was clearly a pro-Trump political campaign ad, running ahead of upcoming midterm elections, with on-screen text boasting about what the president calls his accomplishments. “Largest tax cuts in history” one slogan reads; “Reigniting American manufacturing” another says; “Defend law and order and police” comes next.
The broadcast version of the ad closes with a tribute to Trump from Dana White, the Ultimate Fighting Championship chief executive, who can be heard saying: “He is the toughest, most resilient human being I have ever met in my life.” White used that formulation to describe Trump multiple times during the 2024 presidential election campaign, most notably to sign his praises at the Republican national convention .
Congressman Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat and constitutional scholar, suggested on social media that the ad may violate federal laws including the Hatch Act.
“This may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes,” Raskin wrote . “It is a Hatch Act violation for any government employees who worked on it or used government resources to make it. It is blatantly unethical under numerous federal ethics provisions proscribing the use of government resources for political campaigns.”
AdImpact, a firm that tracks political ads, told the Wall Street Journal that, in addition to Miami, the ad also aired on Fox News in New York, Los Angeles and Washington DC, as well as on Newsmax in Chicago.
JMSN, Detroit-born artist who wrote and performs the song Love Me, wrote on social media that it was used “illegally”, without permission. “I would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign,” the singer wrote. “I am looking at lawyers handling this.”
The images featured in the ad were a bizarre mix of second-term highlights, including flash-frames of: Trump overseeing the US military raid on Venezuela; hosting a state dinner for the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman; accepting the Fifa peace prize; pardoning a turkey; announcing a new class of US Navy ships to be named for himself; attending a Kennedy Center performance; waiting to award the Fifa Club World Cup trophy celebration; showing Cristiano Ronaldo his Presidential Walk of Fame at the White House and addressing McDonalds owners.

Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan are seated at the top table with Trump, his wife Melania, as well as tech executives Elon Musk, Jensen Huang of Nvidia and Tim Cook of Apple.
Others in attendance include: Sam Altman and Greg Brockman of OpenAI; Sergey Brin and Sundar Pichai of Google; Jeff Bezos of Amazon; Mark Zuckerberg of Meta; supreme court justices John Roberts, Amy Coney Barrett and Brett Kavanaugh; Fox hosts Bret Baier, Laura Ingraham and Jesse Watters; David Ellison of Paramount Skydance and Israeli-American Trump donor Miriam Adelson.

articles.title_orig: Iran’s president tells Fox anchor the war was ‘imposed on us’
articles.title_zh: Iran’s president tells Fox anchor the war was ‘imposed on us’
articles.content_orig:
On Feb. 27, the day before the United States and Israel attacked Iran, the American economy was on a steady course to lower inflation and attain greater buying power. Gas was cheap and interest rates were coming down.
Today, none of those things are true anymore. When it comes to the U.S. economy, there’s before the Iran war — and since.
Despite assurances from President Donald Trump as early as March that the war would prove a “short-term excursion,” the conflict is about to round its seventh month. On Tuesday, Trump suggested that a deal could arrive after November’s midterm elections.
The morass has short-circuited Trump’s ability to tout other, more positive economic developments during his second term. The Census Bureau reported last week that the median U.S. household income hit an all-time high in 2025, while the percentage of people in the U.S. living in poverty fell to its lowest level on record. The stock market has done well this year, and the unemployment rate remains low.
Yet, on balance, the negative news has served to obscure the good, both for individual consumers and the nation at large. Before the war, gas prices were just under $3 a gallon. Today they’re at approximately $4.50 on average. Diesel prices went from an average of $3.75 on Feb. 28 to an all-time high of more than $6.50 on Tuesday.
This has caused a domino effect in which inflation rose, then borrowing costs, then mortgage rates.
Surveys of consumer sentiment and presidential approval polls continue to drift lower even as household spending on extras such as travel and dining out remains steady. In March, 35% of respondents to an NBC News poll said Trump had helped the economy. By September, that figure had declined to just 26%.
The White House defended the president’s record in a statement to NBC News.
“President Trump has always been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict, but the Trump administration has remained laser-focused delivering on the President’s long-term economic agenda on the home front,” White House spokesman Kush Desai said in a statement.
The changes wrought by the war are nevertheless unmistakable. With less than six weeks until the midterm elections, the charts below offer the clearest picture yet of the challenge the White House faces as it works to retain Republican control of Congress.
The major reason for inflation’s run-up has been higher energy prices, especially fuel. Prior to the war’s launch, average gas prices stood at just under $3 a gallon, while diesel prices were less than $4 a gallon. Today, gas is nearly $4.50 — its highest ever for late September — and diesel prices continue to set records, most recently hitting $6.52.
Volatile oil price movements have made forecasting their future path nearly impossible. The state of affairs was summed up by oil analysts with JPMorgan in a note published last week: “We simply don’t know how to model the endgame,” they wrote.
When the war began, the analysts said, they assumed the Trump administration wouldn’t let gas prices, inflation or the 10-year Treasury yield move to the levels they have now reached.
“Six months later, many of those lines have been crossed, yet the exit strategy is less clear, not more,” they wrote.
When markets closed Feb. 27, the consumer price index sat at 2.4%, nearly matching its low of the second Trump administration. Today, the CPI, at 3.4%, is a full percentage point higher.
It’s a major reason why the Fed raised interest rates last week for the first time since 2023 , said Kathy Bostjancic, senior vice president and chief economist for Nationwide Mutual.
“The longer inflation is persistently high, the more business and consumers’ expectations for it rise,” she said. “The Fed is trying to make sure they act in a way to avoid bringing that about.”
Last week, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the war was responsible for adding at least 0.5 percentage points to inflation.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury note — a measure of inflation, fiscal risk and economic growth — has climbed from 3.96% to nearly 5% since the war began. It is a major run-up that resembles the one seen in 2022, when pandemic-era inflation began to soar.
While inflation isn’t the only driver of higher yields — borrowing for AI investments has added pressure to the run-up — it is a major one, said Padhraic Garvey, regional head of research for the Americas and managing director at ING Financial Markets.
“At the moment we have inflation, and because we’ve got high inflation, that puts upward pressure on bond yields,” Garvey said.
Increased borrowing costs mean more taxpayer dollars must go toward paying interest, leaving less money available for more socially useful investments.
Alongside the rise in the 10-year yield have been mortgage prices, which closely track its movements. Today the average 30-year mortgage rate stands at more than 7%, compared with less than 6% before the start of the war.
For consumers, high mortgage rates and stubborn inflation have compounded a feeling that many basic necessities are becoming unaffordable. The University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment survey continues to sit near all-time lows. Another measure of consumer confidence from the Conference Board economics consultancy has now declined for two straight months. The theme of affordability has come to dominate midterm House and Senate campaigns, where Democrats are hoping to win over disaffected Republicans and independents in November.
“With a resurgence in fuel prices and trade tensions, consumers anticipate greater pressures on their pocketbooks to come,” Joanne Hsu, director of the University of Michigan Survey of Consumers, wrote this month.
The stock market has charted its own course, largely fueled by ongoing investments in AI. While the index remains just a few percentage points below its all-time high, it has largely stagnated for the past month and closed Friday notching its second straight losing week. That may be a sign that investors may be realizing that there is increasingly no end in sight to the conflict, said Matt Maley, chief strategist at Miller Tabak financial group.
“Eventually the market reacts in a meaningful way once it realizes the situation isn’t going to change,” he said.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.
Joe Murphy is a data editor at NBC News.

Actors detained at Jewish Voice for Peace demonstration against Israeli prime minister’s address to the UN general assembly
Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon and Hacks star Hannah Einbinder were among people detained by police in New York on Thursday as they moved in to break up a protest against Benjamin Netanyahu .
Agence France-Presse footage shows NYPD officers cuffing Thelma & Louise star Sarandon at the demo in the city as the Israeli prime minister was readying to address the United Nations general assembly.
The New York Post reported Einbinder had also been marched away from the demonstration organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, where protesters held banners that read “Stop Arming Israel” and “End the Genocide.”
A spokesperson for the NYPD said officers had responded to reports of an “unscheduled demonstration” where people were blocking an intersection.
“Members of the NYPD Community Affairs Bureau issued … warnings, advising participants that they should leave,” the spokesperson said.
“They continued to block the intersection. Multiple individuals who didn’t comply were taken into custody,” she said, without providing the number of people arrested.
Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and New York ⁠City council member Chi Ossé were also among those arrested.
Inside the general assembly, dozens of envoys from across the world walked out as Netanyahu began his speech, where he assailed both enemies and allies that have crossed him in recent months, including Britain and France, which have recently moved to recognise the state of Palestine.
“They accuse Israel , tiny Israel, of colonialism – some colonialism. And who’s accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God’s sakes, they invented the term,” he told the assembly.
Sarandon, whose movie hits also include The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Dead Man Walking and The Witches of Eastwick, is no stranger to protests over Israel’s war in Gaza.
The US actor told journalists at the Venice film festival this month she was losing work because of her outspoken views.
“I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still. But that’s the power structure,” she said.
“I think there has been a change in terms of the understanding of the situation and the general public, but there are still very strongly held positions within my industry that are held by Zionists and who have not relaxed their feelings towards me.
“But I found my family, I found my people, and I’m OK,” she added.
Einbinder has previously said the cost of not speaking up about Palestine is greater than losing her Hollywood career, citing industry backlash to actors such as Sarandon and Melissa Barrera .
“I think what they know is what I know, which is that the cost of not speaking is higher,” she told Cannes film festival earlier this year.
“There is a greater toll in not speaking and you’ve just got to have your priorities straight. I am under no impression that my small career could ever measure up in comparison to even one human life. It’s an obligation and I will always do it.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Trump praises US-China friendship at state dinner with Xi Jinping
articles.title_zh: Trump praises US-China friendship at state dinner with Xi Jinping
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has thrown China’s leader Xi Jinping a state dinner featuring a tech-heavy guest list, as well as a number of billionaires, Washington powerbrokers, business leaders and the type of festivities that most excite Trump, who has a reputation for reveling in hosting parties.
The dinner on Thursday night wrapped up a day of talks between the two leaders. The summit, Xi’s first visit to Washington in more than a decade, is the second meeting this year between the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies.
Earlier on Thursday, Trump touted what he described as a “great meeting” with Xi, as the two superpowers seek greater dialogue despite differences over issues such as Iran, Taiwan, AI and trade.
“President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” Trump said during his toast on Thursday night, The Associated Press news agency reported.
“Together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations,” Trump added.
Trump has done his best to impress Xi during the Chinese leader’s three-day visit to Washington, and the US president praised their close personal relationship — even as he has decried top Democratic candidates as “communists” ahead of the November midterm elections.
Xi and Trump discussed tensions over Taiwan, trade and artificial intelligence during business hours, all while a First Amendment fight over press access at the White House was unfolding. But Trump publicly chose to focus on showing Xi his White House updates on Thursday afternoon, including letting him tour his Marine One presidential helicopter and a new helipad he built for it, before attention quickly turned to the flashy details of the swanky meal.
At one point, Trump invited dinner guests to tour the site of the new ballroom he is building nearby. Construction projects are a frequent digression for a president who has put a lot of focus on remaking Washington’s physical infrastructure.
Xi noted in his own toast that “President Trump has pledged to make America great again” and that “China is committed to achieving great national rejuvenation”.
“These two goals are both ambitious and can surely be mutually reinforcing,” Xi said.
Those who attended included OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and French luxury goods company LVMH CEO Bernard Arnault.
The dinner came after the president took the unusual step of personally greeting Xi and his wife on Wednesday as they arrived at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington. Normally, presidents wait for their guests to arrive at the White House itself before offering a formal welcome.
